research_text:
## 1. What the finding refers to

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` generates public/private key pairs. Its static `getInstance` methods select a generator by **algorithm name**, optionally with a provider. In the supplied CrySL rule, the reported `ECDH` value refers to the `algorithm` bound by a `Get` event—not to a generated key size or to a `KeyAgreement` call. The message alone does not establish the actual provider, initialization arguments, or consumers of the keys. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

Oracle documents `EC` as a standard **key-pair generator** name and `ECDH` as a standard **key-agreement** name. Its SunEC provider documentation lists them under those respective services. A provider may offer additional names or aliases; the supplied finding does not establish what a particular provider accepts. Sources: [Java standard algorithm names](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html), [JDK 25 provider documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html). ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

## 2. Documented usage and guidance

For conventional EC key generation used with ECDH, the documented service names are `EC` for `KeyPairGenerator` and `ECDH` for `KeyAgreement`. This is documented API guidance, not a determination of the appropriate change for an unidentified use. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3Arc_bumk180724p00001%3Alpd100743723))

The [KeyPairGenerator API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html) documents initialization by key size or by an algorithm-specific parameter specification, optionally with a `SecureRandom`. If initialization is omitted, the provider supplies a documented default; Oracle **recommends explicit initialization** because defaults can differ by provider and change over time. Unsupported generator algorithms and initialization parameters can produce documented exceptions. The API does not prescribe a finding-specific remediation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

The JDK 25 SunEC documentation lists `secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, and `secp521r1` among its recommended curves and documents use of curve names with `ECGenParameterSpec`. It does not establish which curve, provider, or policy applies to this finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3Arc_bumk180724p00001%3Alpd100743723))

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted and wire representations:** `Key.getFormat()` and `getEncoded()` describe a key’s primary encoding, when supported. Oracle identifies X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` and PKCS#8 `PrivateKeyInfo` as standard representations; encoding may be unavailable. `KeyFactory` converts between keys and compatible specifications. These API descriptions do **not** guarantee that changing a generator name or provider preserves an application’s stored bytes or wire format. Sources: [Key API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html), [KeyFactory API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html). ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))
- **Platform support:** Java SE 25 requires EC generator and ECDH agreement support for `secp256r1` and `secp384r1`. Oracle’s JDK 8 SunEC documentation also lists `EC` generation and `ECDH` agreement, with a native-library availability qualification. These statements are version- and provider-specific, not a guarantee for every platform. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
- **Migration path:** The cited API sources do not document an automatic migration for changing an `ECDH` generator request to `EC`. Existing formats, curve parameters, providers, and key consumers remain unresolved.

## 4. What the CrySL source itself states

The supplied [KeyPairGenerator.crysl source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl) declares the governed type as:

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator
```

Its matching event declarations for the reported algorithm value are, verbatim:

```text
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;
```

The source declares `algorithm` as `java.lang.String` and states this constraint, verbatim:

```text
	algorithm in {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"}; //BSI TR-02102-1 Recommends atleast 3000bits for keys
```

Thus, the event declarations distinguish **one- and two-argument** `getInstance` forms and bind the first argument as `algorithm`; the second is written `_`. The file also declares `initialize` events with one or two arguments, and zero-argument `generateKeyPair` and `genKeyPair` events. It states the order `Get, Init, Gen` and additional algorithm-dependent size and prepared-parameter constraints. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**A merely same-named method:** the file declares `SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator`; it does not state a name-only match across arbitrary receiver types. However, the file alone does not specify the analyzer’s method-resolution or receiver-matching implementation, so it is **not sufficient to determine whether a particular analyzer could match an unrelated same-named method**. `getInstance` is static, so it has no instance receiver. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**Source limitation:** the URL points to a mutable branch. The reported rule-pack commit, analyzer version, and correspondence of the supplied SHA-256 to the retrieved file remain unverified. No exact initialization value or runtime diagnostic was supplied, so no key-size conclusion can be drawn.
